stage_description: The senior stage runs from around a year and a half to about two and a half years, since rats typically live only two to three years. Ageing rats slow down, may lose muscle and gain or lose weight, and become more prone to lumps — mammary and other tumours are common in older rats of both sexes — as well as to worsening chronic respiratory disease and cloudy eyes. Care now centres on comfort, close monitoring, and catching problems early.
nutrition: Adjust portions to a slower metabolism while watching closely for unintended weight loss. Offer softer or moistened food if chewing becomes harder, and make sure water is always easy to reach.
activity: Favour gentler enrichment with low ramps, secure footing, and easy access to food, water, and hides. Keep up calm daily interaction and the company of cage-mates while accommodating reduced mobility.
veterinary_check_frequency: Schedule check-ups every six months so a vet can palpate for tumours and monitor breathing, weight, and mobility. Report any new lump promptly rather than waiting for the next visit.
dental_care: Continue offering gnawing items, but if worn or misaligned teeth make chewing difficult, switch to softer foods and have the incisors checked for overgrowth at veterinary visits.
warning_signs: See a vet for lumps or swellings, laboured breathing, rapid weight loss, hind-limb weakness, loss of appetite, or unusual lethargy. Any of these warrants prompt evaluation.
disclaimer: This information is for educational purposes only and does not replace consultation with a veterinarian.
